title: When the Homecoming Turns
premise: Wren Sterling has perfected the art of disappearing at Hollow Creek High, where her mother's fading memory and her father's silence make home a place of unsolvable arguments. When debate coach Mr. Okafor pairs her with her nemesis, Julian Reyes, to document the town's centennial Homecoming tradition, they uncover records proving the beloved festival was built on a buried injustice that could get it shut down. As Wren and Julian race to save Homecoming before the school board votes, she learns that loyalty to a town means nothing without truth—and that her own family history is tangled in what was covered up. In the end, Wren chooses truth over safety, testifying at the board meeting; Homecoming survives only because the town agrees to reinvent it honestly, and Wren finally wins an argument that matters—at home.
about_author: Theo Lockridge is a former high school debate coach who spent six years watching teenagers find their voices in the most unlikely places. He writes stories about small towns, big silences, and the kids brave enough to break them.

chapters.title: The Art of Being Unseen
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. A masterclass in invisibility: perfect grades, closed locker, lunch in the library—until her mother forgets her name at dinner and Wren wins a debate round by refusing to feel anything. Emotional beat: the ache of being excellent everywhere except where it counts.

chapters.title: Nemesis, Assigned
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Mr. Okafor announces semester partners for the Centennial Archive Project: Wren and Julian Reyes, who has tormented her since freshman year. Their first meeting devolves into a fight over who gets to control the narrative. Emotional beat: dread sharpened into defiance.

chapters.title: Rules of Engagement
chapters.summary: Julian's POV. He reveals his own stake: his grandmother was expelled from Hollow Creek High in 1968, and he wants the project to prove the school wronged her. Wren realizes her tidy version of the town may be fiction. Emotional beat: reluctant curiosity replacing contempt.

chapters.title: What Mother Remembers
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Digging through her mother's keepsakes for project material, Wren finds a photo of her mother at the 1998 Homecoming—standing beside Julian's grandmother, both holding protest signs. Her mother doesn't remember why. Emotional beat: the first crack in the family wall.

chapters.title: The Truce
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Wren and Julian negotiate terms like rival nations: shared sources, no sabotage, no talking about the photo. Working late in the archive, they discover the first anomaly—the 1968 Homecoming queen's name scraped from every record. Emotional beat: wary alliance.

chapters.title: Homecoming Week, Interrupted
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The whole town glows with festival prep while Wren and Julian quietly pull threads. A retired teacher warns them off: 'Some traditions cost more than they're worth.' Emotional beat: the vertigo of questioning something everyone loves.

chapters.title: Dorothy Reyes Speaks
chapters.summary: Julian's POV. His grandmother finally tells her story: she was crowned Homecoming queen in 1968, then stripped of the title when the school learned her family had integrated the neighborhood. The town rewrote the record overnight. Emotional beat: grief and fury inherited across generations.

chapters.title: The Argument at Home
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren confronts her parents about the photo; her father shuts down, her mother cries without knowing why. Wren flees to Julian's porch, and for the first time they talk as friends. Emotional beat: loneliness answered, imperfectly.

chapters.title: Evidence, Buried
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. In the newspaper morgue, they find the original 1968 article confirming Dorothy's crowning—and a follow-up 'correction' signed by the school board president: Wren's great-grandfather. Emotional beat: the past reaching into the present with cold fingers.

chapters.title: Loyalty Test
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren's best friend Priya begs her to drop it—Homecoming funds half the school's programs, and the board will kill the festival if the scandal surfaces. Wren must choose between protecting the town and telling the truth. Emotional beat: loyalty revealed as a cage.

chapters.title: Leak
chapters.summary: Julian's POV. Someone tips off the local paper that students are digging; Julian suspects Wren, Wren suspects him, and the truce shatters mid-project. Emotional beat: betrayal—real or imagined—burning down trust.

chapters.title: The Other Side of Invisible
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Ostracized by classmates who blame her for threatening Homecoming, Wren experiences what visibility costs. Her mother, in a lucid moment, says: 'I marched because staying quiet felt worse.' Emotional beat: inheritance of courage.

chapters.title: Rebuilding the Case
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Wren and Julian reconcile—not with an apology but with evidence: Dorothy's confiscated crown, found boxed in the school attic. They decide to present everything at the board's centennial vote. Emotional beat: partnership forged in purpose.

chapters.title: Pressure
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The board chair offers Wren a deal: full scholarship endorsement if the project stays 'celebratory.' Her father, a school employee, could lose his job. Emotional beat: temptation wearing a friendly face.

chapters.title: What Winning Costs
chapters.summary: Julian's POV. Julian nearly takes a separate deal to restore his grandmother's name quietly, erasing the larger injustice. Dorothy herself refuses: 'Don't win me a trophy. Win me the truth.' Emotional beat: pride confronted and dismantled.

chapters.title: The Night Before
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren drafts her board testimony, then practices the argument at her kitchen table—against her father, against the town, against herself. Her mother listens and, briefly lucid, adds a missing detail from 1968. Emotional beat: fear transmuted into resolve.

chapters.title: The Board Meeting
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. The climax: Wren and Julian present the archive—crown, articles, testimony—as the room erupts. The board moves to cancel Homecoming entirely rather than reform it. Wren delivers her final argument: a tradition built on a lie isn't worth saving; one rebuilt on truth is. Emotional beat: the argument of her life.

chapters.title: Vote
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Deadlocked, the board yields when Dorothy Reyes walks in and speaks. They vote to continue Homecoming—with the 1968 record restored and Dorothy's crown displayed permanently. Emotional beat: victory that feels like relief, not triumph.

chapters.title: Aftermath
chapters.summary: Julian's POV. The town splits between gratitude and resentment; Priya comes around; Mr. Okafor gives them top marks and a warning about how much harder real advocacy gets. Emotional beat: the sobering morning after courage.

chapters.title: The Argument at Home, Revisited
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren and her father finally have the fight they've avoided for years—and finish it. He admits his silence was inherited too. It isn't fixed, but it's honest. Emotional beat: reconciliation without a bow on it.

chapters.title: Homecoming
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. The reimagined festival opens with Dorothy's story told aloud, her crown carried in the procession. Wren and Julian stand together, no longer nemesis or partner but something new. Emotional beat: belonging earned, not granted.

chapters.title: Head Up, Voice On
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Epilogue: Wren signs up for the state debate final with a case about her own town, locker open, mother's photo inside. She's done winning arguments that don't matter. Emotional beat: identity claimed—visible, imperfect, unafraid.
